title: Witness encryption from plain LWE
formal: Assuming the specified polynomial-modulus decisional LWE hardness, does every polynomial-time NP witness relation admit standard-model witness encryption with correctness for valid witnesses and message indistinguishability on false instances?
definitions:
The security parameter is lambda, supplied in unary. Efficient algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; security is against nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-size circuit families with polynomially many oracle queries. A function is negligible if it is eventually smaller than lambda^{-c} for every constant c>0. All message, instance and witness lengths in a security experiment are polynomial in lambda. No random oracle, trusted hardware or additional computational assumption is available.

The selected plain-LWE assumption is decisional LWE in dimension lambda, with q the least prime at least lambda^3 and integer error distribution assigning probability proportional to exp(-pi e^2/lambda^2) to each e in Z, reduced modulo q. For every polynomial m(lambda), a uniform matrix A in Z_q^{m by lambda}, a uniform secret s in Z_q^lambda and independent errors e give (A,As+e) computationally indistinguishable from (A,u) with uniform independent u in Z_q^m. Hardness is against the circuit adversaries above with negligible distinguishing advantage. This explicitly fixes polynomial modulus and inverse-polynomial relative noise; it does not assume evasive LWE, subexponential security or leakage resilience. It is an editorial parameter choice, not a claim that every formulation called LWE is equivalent.

For a fixed polynomial-time relation R(x,w) with a polynomial witness-length bound, let L_R={x: some w satisfies R(x,w)}. A scheme consists of Enc_R(1^lambda,x,m;r) and Dec_R(1^lambda,x,c,w). Runtime and ciphertext length are polynomial in the explicit inputs and security parameter. There is no key-generation or setup secret: x is the public encryption instance. Correctness requires that whenever R(x,w)=1, decrypting an honestly generated ciphertext returns m except with negligible probability, uniformly over valid polynomial-size x,w,m.

False-instance security means that for every polynomial-size sequence x_lambda outside L_R, any two equal-length polynomial-size messages m0_lambda,m1_lambda, and any adversarial auxiliary strings of polynomial length, the encryptions of the two messages at x_lambda are computationally indistinguishable to the adversary given x_lambda and those strings. No confidentiality is required on true instances lacking a known witness. The implication allows non-black-box constructions and reductions; a separation limited to a particular use of LWE is not a refutation of the unrestricted implication.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked construction and a reduction from every violation of correctness or false-instance security to the stated assumptions, or prove a genuine impossibility of the implication. A candidate supported only by evasive LWE or obfuscation assumptions is insufficient. Black-box-only barriers must be described as restricted barriers.
context:
The original witness-encryption definition protects messages when the public NP instance is false and permits witness-based decryption when it is true.

The evasive-LWE construction uses an additional assumption whose auxiliary-information guarantee is not included in ordinary decisional LWE.
why: This asks for the minimal assumptions needed to encrypt against the existence of mathematical witnesses.

import_provenance.original_statement: Can witness encryption for every NP relation be built from ordinary LWE hardness alone? A satisfying witness must decrypt, while encryptions of different messages must be indistinguishable whenever the public NP statement is false.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: Editorial continuation of Sahai’s introduction of witness encryption. Evasive-LWE constructions use an additional assumption; this target is weaker than full obfuscation, so solving it need not solve the preceding problem.
